instruction:
Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (braced form, `module zig_codegen { ... }`) for the compiler's Zig backend. Import the AST spec with `using ast: @import("../../../ast.t27")`.

Define `CodegenOptions` (emit_comments, emit_debug, optimize_level, target_triple, include_runtime) and a `ZigCodegen` struct holding the Program AST, options, a StringBuilder output, indent_level, an error list and a t27-symbol -> zig-symbol map. `new(ast, opts)` constructs it; `generate()` drives the whole emission in order: header, imports, constants, data section, code section, the spec test blocks when a spec_decl is present, then the test / invariant / bench sections and a footer.

The code section must emit the VSA helpers `vsa_bind` and `vsa_bundle2` as literal Zig text, then `pub fn execute()` with a 27-entry Coptic register file where r26 is the hard-wired zero register, followed by label constants and one emitter per opcode: MOV, JZ, JNZ, JMP, MUL, ADD, SUB, BIND, BUNDLE, HALT.

Also provide `generate_conformance()` producing a JSON test-vector document from the test cases, spec test blocks (given/when/then clauses) and invariants; operand/label/opcode-to-Zig converters; `emit_type_for_value` picking u8/i32/i64 by magnitude; `mangle_name` and `mangle_test_name` producing valid Zig identifiers (no leading digit); indent/dedent helpers; a StringBuilder; the simplified AST types the generator consumes; and an `int_to_str` helper.

Close with TDD-inside-spec tests covering construction, header emission, instruction emission, each of the three emitted sections, opcode mnemonics and both mangling functions; invariants recording the 27-register file, the always-zero r26, non-negative indent level and valid conformance JSON; and benches with latency targets for generate, emit_instruction and operand_to_zig.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect using the semicolon module form (`module ZeroDSP_MAC;`) for the ZeroDSP FPGA multiply-accumulate unit. Use base::types, base::ops and isa::registers.

Configuration: MAC_WIDTH = 27 trits per operand, MAC_ACC_BITS = 32, NUM_MAC_UNITS = 8, PIPELINE_STAGES = 4; opcodes OP_MAC_MUL/MAC/MACC/DOT and status constants READY/BUSY/DONE.

Ternary multiplication must be table-driven: a 9-entry `MAC_LUT : [9]i8` indexed by (a+1)*3 + (b+1) over balanced trits, so (-1,-1) and (+1,+1) give +1, (+1,-1) gives -1, and anything involving 0 gives 0. Document the index mapping in comments.

Declare a `MACUnit` struct (accumulator, status, pipeline registers) and a module-level array of NUM_MAC_UNITS of them.

Functions: `extract_trit` / `pack_trit` for the 2-bit-per-trit packing (0 -> 0, 1 -> +1, 2 -> -1); `mac_multiply` (LUT product packed back into a TernaryWord); `mac_cycle` (accumulate the trit-wise dot product into a signed accumulator); `mac_dot_product` over vectors; `mac_matrix_vector` with a per-row unit assignment; `mac_parallel_multiply` round-robining across units; and unit management: status read/write, reset, reset_all, get/set accumulator. Every function taking a unit index must bound-check it and return a safe sentinel.

Tests must cover the four LUT sign combinations, the configuration constants, accumulation with and without an initial accumulator, dot products including a cancelling negative case, status transitions, reset behaviour, an out-of-range unit index, a 2x2 matrix-vector product, trit extract/pack roundtrip, and parallel independence. Add invariants for the LUT size and entries, the constants, status range, reset semantics, result width and unit independence, plus latency benches for multiply, cycle, dot product, extract_trit, status read, reset, parallel multiply and matrix-vector.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module Hir { ... }`) defining a Hardware Intermediate Representation that decouples .t27 semantics from Verilog/SystemVerilog emission. The parser has no Vec or generics, so every container must be a fixed-size array plus a count field.

Capacities: MAX_PORTS 64, MAX_SIGNALS 256, MAX_ASSIGNS 256, MAX_INSTANCES 32, MAX_ERRORS 64, MAX_MEMS 16, MAX_MEM_PORTS 4, MAX_CLOCK_DOMAINS 8, MAX_BUS_PORTS 8.

Enums (all `enum(i8)`): Edge (posedge/negedge/comb), PortDir, SignalKind (wire/reg), MemKind (bram/dram/rom), MemPortMode, CdcStrategy (two_flop, async_fifo, handshake, gray_code), BusKind (axi4_lite, axi4_full, apb, wishbone).

Structs: Port, Signal, Assign, Instance, MemPort, Mem, ClockDomain, BusPort, and a flat `HirModule` carrying all of those arrays with their counts.

Provide `empty_*` sentinel constructors for every node type, `make_port` / `make_signal` / `make_mem` / `make_clock_domain` / `make_bus_port`, and mutation helpers (`add_port`, `add_signal`, `add_assign`, `add_instance`, `add_mem`, `add_clock_domain`, `add_bus_port`) that copy the module, append only if under the capacity, and return the new value. Add `mem_add_port`, `mem_total_bits`, `mem_bram18_count` (ceiling division by 18*1024), and `bus_port_total_signals` with the AXI4-Lite and APB signal counts. Query helpers: port/signal/assign counts, `has_clock_port`, `has_reset_port`, `total_port_bits`. `validate_module` returns an error count for an empty module name and for duplicate port or signal names.

Cover it with tests for empty construction, each add helper, clock/reset detection, validation success and both failure modes, memory bit and BRAM18 math, memory ports, and clock-domain and bus-port attachment; invariants for empty-module zero counts, non-negative counts, memory port bounds and positive bus signal counts; and benches for BRAM18 estimation and module construction.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module Stdlib { ... }`) describing the T27 FPGA standard-library IP catalog with resource-utilisation estimates. Use flat arrays plus count fields only, since the parser has no Vec or generics.

Define `IpKind` as an `enum(i8)` covering uart_tx, uart_rx, spi_master, spi_slave, i2c_master, gpio, pwm, timer, bram_ctrl, axi_interconnect, clock_crossing, gf16_alu and ternary_alu. Define `ResourceEstimate` (luts, ffs, bram18, dsp48, io_pins), `IpCore` (name, kind, version, resources, clock_freq_mhz, vendor, verified), `IpCatalog` (name, a 32-entry cores array, core_count) and `BoardResources`.

Constructors: `zero_resources`, `resources(...)`, `ip_core(...)` defaulting version to 1 and vendor to "t27" with verified false, `empty_catalog(name)` filling all 32 slots with blank cores, and two board profiles — arty_a7 (33800 LUTs, 67600 FFs, 60 BRAM18, 90 DSP48, 210 IO) and xc7a100t (63400 / 126800 / 135 / 240 / 300).

Query functions must sum LUTs, FFs, BRAM18 and DSP48 over the first core_count entries, and provide `fits_board`, `luts_remaining` (clamped at zero) and `utilization_percent` (guarding a zero-LUT board). `validate_ip` returns an error count for an empty name or a zero clock frequency.

Tests should cover both constructors, catalog creation, LUT totalling for a one-core catalog, both board profiles, fits/utilisation on an empty catalog, the two validation failures, empty totals, remaining LUTs on a full board and the IpCore defaults. Add invariants that the board profiles have positive LUTs, that zero_resources is all zero, and that an empty catalog totals zero, plus a fits_board latency bench.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module PackedTrit { ... }`) specifying a 5-trits-per-byte packed balanced-ternary encoding. Import base::types, base::ops and numeric::gf16 rather than re-declaring anything they own.

Constants: TRIT_NEG/-1, TRIT_ZERO/0, TRIT_POS/1 as i8; TRITS_PER_BYTE 5, MAX_PACKED_BYTES 2400, MAX_TRITS 12000; the 2-bit encoding ENCODED_ZERO 0, ENCODED_POS 1, ENCODED_NEG 2 and TRIT_MASK 0x03.

Types: `PackResult` (bytes, count, valid), `UnpackResult` (trits, count, valid), `PackedBigInt` (data, sign, magnitude) and `ArithResult` (value, overflow).

The encoding and big-integer entry points are declared as signatures only, each carrying a doc comment stating the algorithm, the validity or overflow rule, and the complexity: `encodePack`, `decodePack`, `packed_add`, `packed_sub`, `packed_mul`, `packed_from_i64`, `packed_to_i64`. Give full bodies only for the three utilities: `trit_valid`, `normalize_trit` (clamping out-of-range values to the nearest valid trit) and `count_trits` (byte count times TRITS_PER_BYTE).

Write the tests in given/when/then form: single-trit and multi-trit packing, an invalid trit forcing valid=false with count 0, the empty input, the maximum trit count, encode/decode roundtrips, additive and multiplicative identities on PackedBigInt, positive/negative/zero i64 conversion, trit validation and normalisation, and count_trits for zero, one and three bytes. Add invariants asserting the trit constants are in range, the encoding values fit two bits, TRIT_MASK is 0x03 and MAX_TRITS == MAX_PACKED_BYTES * TRITS_PER_BYTE, plus latency and throughput benches for every declared operation.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module BrainSummaries { ... }`) for Ring 061, the Queen brain's episode-summarisation pipeline. Use queen::lotus for the Episode type, the OUTCOME_* codes and the QUALITY_* codes.

Config: MAX_EPISODES_PER_SUMMARY 50, SUMMARY_RETENTION_DAYS 90, MIN_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD 0.5, and summary-type codes for daily, weekly, ring and phase.

Define a `BrainSummary` struct grouping identity and date range, episode and cycle counts, average confidence, domain-health metrics, learning metrics (new and updated patterns), cycle-time statistics (avg / max / min in ms) and an overall quality byte with a fixed-size reason buffer. Also define a `SummaryIndex` with per-type counts and the last summary id.

`aggregate_episodes(episodes, summary_type)` walks the episodes once, counting success and failure outcomes, summing confidence, tracking max and min cycle time (min seeded to the u64 maximum), then divides to get the averages — guarded against an empty episode list — and finishes by calling `determine_quality`. `determine_quality` maps success rate and average confidence onto QUALITY_GOOD (>= 0.9 and >= 0.8), QUALITY_UNSTABLE (>= 0.7 and >= 0.6) or QUALITY_BAD. Add `save_summary` / `load_summary` stubs documenting the on-disk path pattern, and `generate_daily_summary`, `generate_ring_summary` and `generate_phase_summary` that filter episodes and stamp the relevant date range, ring range or phase number.

Tests must cover the empty aggregation, an all-success aggregation reaching QUALITY_GOOD, a mixed batch where partial outcomes count in neither bucket, and all three quality bands. Add invariants that totals stay consistent, average confidence stays in [0,1], successes never exceed total cycles and max cycle time is at least min, plus benches for aggregating 50 episodes and for the quality decision.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module TernaryMemory { ... }`) for Ring 066, defining how trits are stored and accessed in memory. Use base::types.

Constants: the three trit values; TRIT_CAPACITY 27 trits per word, WORD_CAPACITY 1024 words, PAGE_SIZE 256; and cell states FREE, ALLOCATED, LOCKED, DIRTY.

Three layers, each with an init function:
- `TritCell` (value, state, last_access, access_count). `trit_cell_write` refuses to write a LOCKED cell, otherwise stores the value, marks the cell DIRTY, stamps last_access and bumps access_count; `trit_cell_read` also stamps and bumps before returning the value.
- `TernaryWord` (an array of TRIT_CAPACITY cells, a state and a checksum). `ternary_word_write_trit` bounds-checks the index, refuses a locked word, and on success marks the word DIRTY and recomputes the checksum; `ternary_word_read_trit` returns TRIT_ZERO out of bounds. `compute_checksum` is a position-weighted sum over the cells.
- `TernaryMemoryBank` (WORD_CAPACITY words, an allocated counter, total_accesses). Provide bump-pointer `ternary_memory_alloc` returning an all-ones sentinel when full, `ternary_memory_free`, and read/write entry points that increment total_accesses first and then bounds-check the word index.

Add `get_timestamp` (placeholder returning 0) and `validate_trit`.

Tests should cover cell init, write/read roundtrip for both signs, the locked-cell refusal, word init, per-trit write/read, the out-of-bounds path, bank init, alloc/free index sequencing and a bank-level write/read. Add invariants that reads and writes each increment access_count, that writing a trit changes the word checksum, that allocation is monotonic, that every bank access increments total_accesses, and that a word goes FREE -> DIRTY on first write. Finish with benches for cell writes, word reads, bank accesses and checksum computation.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module JonesPolynomial { ... }`) computing the Jones polynomial of a link from its crossing structure, V(L,t) = (-t^(-3/4))^w(L) * <L>, where <L> is the Kauffman bracket. Use math::constants for PHI.

Represent a link as an array of crossing signs, +1 or -1 (CROSSING_POSITIVE / CROSSING_NEGATIVE). `writhe` is their sum. `bracket_parameter(t)` returns A = t^(-1/4), and BRACKET_UNKNOT is 1.0.

`bracket_from_crossings(crossings, t)` counts positive and negative crossings and returns the known closed forms: 1 for the unknot, -A^7 - A^3 for the all-positive trefoil, -A^-7 - A^-3 for the negative trefoil, A^8 - A^4 + 1 - A^-4 + A^-8 for the figure-eight (two positive and two negative crossings), and A^(pos-neg) otherwise. `jones_polynomial_from_structure` combines writhe and bracket; keep a legacy `jones_polynomial(t, bracket, w)` taking them directly. Add `jones_trefoil(t)` over three positive crossings and `jones_trefoil_at_phi()`, documenting that V(trefoil, phi) should come out near phi^2 + 1.

The module is self-contained numerically, so also implement `pow` (fast integer exponentiation, series expansion for fractional exponents, NaN for a negative base with a fractional exponent), `ln` via the atanh series, `floor`, `isnan` and `isinf`.

Write given/when/then tests for writhe on empty, single-sign, mixed and trefoil inputs; the bracket parameter at phi and at 2.0; the trefoil-at-phi identity within 0.1; the unknot bracket; a negative exponent in pow; the structural Jones value for trefoil and unknot; that different t give different V; and that results are neither NaN nor infinite. Add prose invariants for the phi relation, writhe additivity, unknot normalisation and Reidemeister invariance, plus cycle-budget benches for writhe, the trefoil evaluation and the bracket parameter.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module BoardMinimalXC7A100T { ... }`) describing a minimal board profile for the QMTECH XC7A100T-CSG324: a heartbeat LED bank plus UART loopback, using only prjxray-verified pins. Use base::types and base::ops.

Board constants: BOARD_NAME "QMTECH XC7A100T-CSG324", FPGA_FAMILY "artix7", FPGA_PART "xc7a100tcsg324-1", a 12 MHz clock with an 83 ns period, IO_STANDARD "LVCMOS33", CONFIG_VOLTAGE "3.3", NUM_LEDS 8, HAS_UART true, HAS_SPI false, HAS_MAC_DEBUG false.

Define `PinAssignment` (port name, package pin, iostandard, is_clock / is_input / is_output flags, bank) and `ClockConstraint` (port name, period_ns, waveform_high_ns, freq_hz). Declare one const PinAssignment per physical pin — clk on E3, rst_n on C18, uart_rx on T14, uart_tx on T15, and led[0..7] on H17, K15, J13, N14, R18, U18, T13, T11, with clk and reset in bank 0 and the LEDs in bank 1 — plus the system ClockConstraint. Collect the twelve pins into one array and the single clock into another.

Functions: count_pins, count_clocks, count_leds, has_uart, has_spi, `is_prjxray_verified` matching the twelve known package pins, and `find_pin_by_port` returning an all-empty PinAssignment on a miss.

Tests must check each named constant, the counts, the package pin and direction flags of clk, rst_n, both UART pins and LEDs 0 and 7, the clock constraint's consistency, lookup by port name including the miss case, and prjxray verification for the clock, reset and all eight LEDs. Add invariants that the identity strings are non-empty, the clock frequency and period are positive, the IO standard and config voltage match, SPI and MAC debug stay off, the LED count matches, total pins equal 4 + NUM_LEDS, clk is a clock input, and the UART and LED directions are right. Close with lookup and verification latency benches.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module ApbBridge { ... }`) for an APB register-mapped peripheral bridge in the Trinity T27 FPGA HIR. Keep everything parser-compatible: flat arrays plus count fields, no Vec or generics.

Constants: APB_ADDR_WIDTH 32, APB_DATA_WIDTH 32, APB_STRB_WIDTH 4, and an `ApbTransfer` `enum(i8)` of idle / setup / access.

Structs: `ApbConfig` (name, addr_width, data_width, num_peripherals, base_addr, addr_mask, has_pslverr, has_pprot), `PeripheralMap` (name, base_addr, size, index), and simulation-side `ApbRequest` (addr, wdata, write, strb, valid) and `ApbResponse` (rdata, ready, slverr).

Constructors: `apb_bridge(...)` with the error/protection flags off, `apb_bridge_with_error(...)` with both on, `peripheral_map(...)`, `apb_read_request` (full strobes, not a write), `apb_write_request`, `apb_ok_response` and `apb_error_response`.

Queries: `strb_width` = data_width / 8; `addr_bits_for_peripherals` = log2 of the peripheral count, zero for a single peripheral; `peripheral_addr_offset` shifting the index by that many bits; `is_read` / `is_write` (both requiring valid); `apb_port_count` summing the APB signal set with the optional PSLVERR and 3-bit PPROT; and `select_peripheral` scanning up to sixteen maps for the range containing an address and returning 65535 on a miss. `validate_apb` returns an error count for an empty name, a zero address or data width, a data width that is not byte-aligned, or zero peripherals; `validate_peripheral_map` checks the name and a non-zero size.

Write given/when/then tests for both constructors, strobe widths at 32 and 16 bits, address bits for 1 / 4 / 8 peripherals, read and write requests, both responses, all four validation failures plus the success case, both map validations and a positive port count. Add invariants on address width, byte alignment, the strobe/data relationship, positive peripheral count and non-negative validation, plus a validation latency bench.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module HwTypes { ... }`) defining the signal-level hardware type system for the Trinity T27 FPGA HIR, with bit-accurate widths and explicit signedness.

Declare `ResetKind` (async / sync), `ResetPolarity` (active high / low) and a `HwTypeTag` `enum(i8)` numbering bits, uint, sint, bool, clock, reset, vector, bundle, enum and gf16 from 0 to 9. Because the parser has no sum types, represent a type as one flat `HwType` struct: tag, width, is_signed_flag, is_clock_flag, is_reset_flag, elem_tag, vec_len, field_count.

Provide constructors `hw_bits(w)`, `hw_uint(w)`, `hw_sint(w)` (signed), `hw_bool()`, `hw_clock()`, `hw_reset()` (all width 1, with the appropriate flag set), `hw_vector(elem, len)` whose width is the element width times the length and which inherits the element's signedness and tag, and `hw_gf16()` at width 16.

Queries: `hw_width`, `is_signed`, `is_clock_like`, `is_reset_like`. `types_equal` is structural over width and the three flags. `verilog_range` reports whether a range declaration is needed (width > 1). `is_connectable(target, source)` requires equal widths and matching clock and reset flags.

Cover it with given/then tests for the width of each constructor including nested vectors, signedness for uint / sint / bool, clock-like and reset-like detection, structural equality on identical, different-width and different-signedness types, and connectability including a width mismatch and a clock-versus-bool mismatch. Add invariants pinning bool and clock to width 1, gf16 to 16, uint unsigned and sint signed, non-negative and monotonic widths, the vector width product, and reflexive connectability. Finish with latency benches for hw_width and is_clock_like.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module ZeroDSP_UART { ... }`) for the ZeroDSP FPGA debug UART. Use base::types, base::ops and isa::registers.

Constants: a 100 MHz UART clock, 115200 baud, a derived UART_BIT_PERIOD, an 8-bit width, a 16-deep FIFO, and status codes IDLE 0, TX_BUSY 1, RX_BUSY 2, ERROR 3.

Declare a `UARTState` struct (tx_data, tx_valid, tx_ready, rx_data, rx_valid, rx_error, bit_counter, status) and a module-level instance initialised idle with tx_ready true; and a `UARTConfig` struct (baud_divisor, parity_enable, stop_bits, fifo_enable) initialised from the clock and baud rate with a 16x oversampling divisor, parity off, one stop bit and the FIFO on.

Functions: `uart_tx_ready`; `uart_tx_send(data)` returning false when the transmitter is not ready and otherwise latching the byte, asserting tx_valid, clearing tx_ready and moving to TX_BUSY; `uart_rx_ready`; `uart_rx_read` which clears rx_valid and returns the byte; `uart_status`; `uart_reset` restoring every state field to its initial value; and `uart_configure` overwriting the four config fields.

Write the tests in the given/then style: the initial idle status, initial tx readiness, initial rx invalidity, a successful send, a second send being refused while busy, reset restoring both status and tx readiness, reconfiguration of the divisor and of parity / stop bits / FIFO, the derived bit period, the constant block, the full state change after a send, that reading clears rx_valid, and that reset clears rx_error and the bit counter. Add invariants that the status is always one of the four codes and that tx_ready holds exactly when the status is IDLE, plus nanosecond latency benches for uart_tx_ready, uart_rx_ready and uart_reset.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module TernarySorting { ... }`) for Ring 080: sorting operations over balanced-ternary data. Use base::types and declare TRIT_NEG, TRIT_ZERO and TRIT_POS as i32.

Functions, all operating on `[]i32` slices:
- `sort_compare(a, b) i32` returning a trit: -1 when a < b, +1 when a > b, 0 when equal.
- `bubble_sort` — O(n^2) with a swapped flag for early exit and a shrinking upper bound.
- `selection_sort` — O(n^2), swapping only when the minimum index moved.
- `insertion_sort` — O(n^2), stable, shifting elements right until the key's slot is found.
- `quick_sort(data, lo, hi)` — in-place Lomuto partition on the high pivot, recursing on both halves and guarding the underflow when the pivot lands at index 0.
- `is_sorted` — true when the slice is non-decreasing.

Write the tests in the brace form used by this dialect, with `try eq(...)`, `try is_sorted(...)` and `try not(...)`: bubble sort over a five-element trit array ending with -1 first and +1 last and reported sorted, selection sort over three trits, insertion sort producing a sorted result, is_sorted rejecting unsorted input, and the ordering of sort_compare across all three outcomes. Add an invariant that a hand-written non-decreasing trit array satisfies is_sorted and another that sort_compare is antisymmetric, then a bench that fills a 27-element array with cycling trit values and bubble-sorts it.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module Api { ... }`) defining the API client's message and response types. This is the source of truth for those types — the note at the top should record that no business logic lives in the Rust side. Use base::types.

Declare `MessageRole` (User 0, Assistant 1, System 2) and `ContentBlockType` (Text 0, ToolUse 1, ToolResult 2, Thinking 3) as explicitly numbered enums. Declare a `Message` struct pairing a role with content, and one struct per content block: `TextBlock` (text), `ToolUseBlock` (id, name, input), `ToolResultBlock` (tool_use_id, content) and `ThinkingBlock` (thinking) — each carrying its block_type tag.

Declare `Usage` (input_tokens, output_tokens) and `ApiResponse` (id, model, stop_reason, usage).

Constants: DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 30, DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS 8192, plus the default base URL and model string.

Helper functions: `get_block_type_name` mapping the four block types to "text", "tool_use", "tool_result" and "thinking" with an "unknown" fallback; `get_role_name` mapping the three roles to "user", "assistant" and "system" with the same fallback; and `total_usage` summing the two token counts.

Finish with named `test "..."` blocks using assert: one checking all four block-type names, one checking all three role names, one constructing a Usage with 100 input and 50 output tokens and asserting the total is 150, and one asserting the two numeric constants.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module GFCrossLanguageConformance { ... }`) that pins the GoldenFloat cross-language conformance contract: every backend must produce identical bits for identical inputs. Import math::constants and the gf16 and gf32 FFI surfaces.

The module is test-only — no functions of its own, just numbered `test` blocks using const bindings and a `then` clause. Cover, in order:

1. phi encoded through gf32_from_f64 must equal the reference constant 0x3FCF1BBD.
2. phi encoded in both widths must have sign 0 and a positive exponent under the extract helpers.
3. A roundtrip over a small table of values (1.618, 3.14159, 2.71828, 1.0, -1.0, 0.5) through gf16_from_f64 / gf16_to_f64 must stay within 0.01.
4. Classification: gf16_is_zero on an encoded 0.0, gf16_is_inf on a very large value, gf16_is_nan on 0xFFFF, and gf16_is_nan false for zero.
5. Arithmetic: gf16_add of encoded 1.0 and 0.618 decodes within 0.01 of 1.618.
6. The FPGA-safety contract — encode and decode work on u16/u32 only, no f64 in compute — checked by a zero roundtrip that also reports gf16_is_zero.
7. Mantissa extraction of phi in both widths is non-zero, with a comment noting the two formats allocate mantissa bits differently.
8. Special values: zero and negative zero both roundtrip and both classify as zero.

State the reference constant in the header comment.

Write a t27 testbench spec in the module dialect (`module GF16_Accel_Testbench { ... }`) exercising the GF16 accelerator through `fpga::gf16_accel::Gf16Accel`. This is the testbench dialect used elsewhere under specs/fpga/testbench: module-level `var` signals, a `tick`/`reset` pair, plain `test` blocks whose assertions are `invariant` statements, standalone module-level invariants, and a `bench` block.

Constants: CLK_PERIOD 20, SIM_TIMEOUT 5_000_000, PHI_TOLERANCE 3.

Signals: clk, rst_n, 16-bit op_a / op_b, an 8-bit op_code, start, a 16-bit result, valid, busy, plus test_passed and test_failed counters.

`tick` toggles the clock low then high; `reset` holds rst_n low for two ticks, releases it and ticks once more. Add three driver functions — gf16_add, gf16_mul and gf16_mac — each of which loads the operands, selects op_code 0, 1 or 2, pulses start for one tick and spins on `valid` before returning the result.

Tests: reset leaves valid and busy low; adding encoded 1.0 (0x3C00) and zero gives a non-zero result; multiplying 0x3C00 by itself returns 0x3C00; multiplying by zero returns zero; a MAC over a prior product is non-zero; addition and multiplication are both commutative across 0x4000 and 0x3C00; and squaring the phi encoding 0x3E80 is non-zero. Add a module-level invariant that PHI_TOLERANCE is positive, and a throughput bench that resets and then runs one hundred multiplications by 0x3C00.

Write a t27 testbench spec in the module dialect (`module Bridge_Testbench { ... }`) for the FPGA bridge exposed as `fpga::bridge::FPGA_Bridge`, covering data streaming, packet framing and cross-domain transfers. Follow the testbench dialect used elsewhere under specs/fpga/testbench: module-level `var` signals, a `tick`/`reset` pair, `test` blocks whose assertions are written as `invariant` statements, standalone module-level invariants, and a `bench` block.

Constants: CLK_PERIOD 20, SIM_TIMEOUT 5_000_000, BRIDGE_WIDTH 32, FIFO_DEPTH 8.

Signals: clk, rst_n, the transmit side (tx_valid, tx_data, tx_ready), the receive side (rx_valid, rx_data, rx_ready), bridge_busy and bridge_error, plus test_passed and test_failed counters.

`send_packet(data)` returns false immediately when tx_ready is low; otherwise it asserts tx_valid with the data, ticks, waits for bridge_busy to rise, deasserts tx_valid, waits for busy to fall, and reports success as the absence of bridge_error. `receive_packet()` raises rx_ready, spins until rx_valid, captures the word, drops rx_ready and returns the data.

Tests: after reset the bridge is neither busy nor errored and rx_valid is low; a single 0xDEAD transfer succeeds without error; eight successive transfers leave no error; with rx_ready held low a transfer still leaves rx_valid asserted before the consumer catches up; and both the all-ones and all-zeros words transfer successfully. Add module-level invariants that BRIDGE_WIDTH and FIFO_DEPTH are positive, and a throughput bench sending one hundred packets after reset.

Write a t27 testbench spec in the module dialect (`module Stdlib_Testbench { ... }`) exercising the FPGA standard library through `fpga::stdlib::Stdlib` — the IP core catalog, parameter validation and helper maths. Follow the testbench dialect used elsewhere under specs/fpga/testbench: module-level `var` signals, a `tick`/`reset` pair, `test` blocks whose assertions are written as `invariant` statements, standalone module-level invariants, and a `bench` block.

Constants: CLK_PERIOD 20, MAX_IP_CORES 32, MAX_PARAMS 8. Signals: clk, rst_n, ip_valid, plus test_passed and test_failed counters. `tick` toggles the clock; `reset` holds rst_n low for two ticks, releases it and ticks once more.

Implement the four parameter helpers the IP generators rely on: `clog2` returning 0 for inputs of 0 or 1 and otherwise the ceiling log2 computed by shifting value-1 down to zero; `max_val`; `min_val`; and `clamp(val, lo, hi)`.

Tests: reset leaves ip_valid low; clog2 of 1, 2, 4 and 256 gives 0, 1, 2 and 8; max_val and min_val each checked on two ordered pairs; and clamp checked in range, below the lower bound and above the upper bound. Add a module-level invariant that MAX_IP_CORES is positive, and a bench that resets and then runs one hundred iterations calling all four helpers.

Write a t27 testbench spec in the module dialect (`module VCD_Trace_Testbench { ... }`) for the waveform dump generator exposed as `fpga::vcd_trace::VcdTrace`, covering signal hierarchy and timestamp management. Follow the testbench dialect used elsewhere under specs/fpga/testbench: module-level `var` signals, a `tick`/`reset` pair, `test` blocks whose assertions are written as `invariant` statements, standalone module-level invariants, and a `bench` block.

Constants: CLK_PERIOD 20, MAX_SIGNALS 256, TIMESTAMP_RES_PS 10.

Signals: clk, rst_n, trace_en, signal_count, timestamp_ps, dump_complete, plus test_passed and test_failed counters.

Unlike the other testbenches here, `tick` also advances simulated time: it toggles the clock and adds TIMESTAMP_RES_PS to timestamp_ps. `reset` holds rst_n low for two ticks, releases it and ticks once. Add `advance_time(steps)` looping tick that many times and returning the current timestamp, and `format_timestamp(ps)` converting picoseconds to nanoseconds by dividing by 1000.

Tests: after reset both trace_en and dump_complete are false; advancing ten steps from a zeroed timestamp yields 100 ps; formatting 10000 ps yields 10 ns; and the two configuration constants hold their expected values. Add module-level invariants that MAX_SIGNALS and TIMESTAMP_RES_PS are positive, and a bench that resets, enables tracing, advances one hundred steps and disables tracing again.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module TriComputeChallenge { ... }`) adding the fraud proof and slashing layer on top of TRI-NET compute settlement. Open with the motivation: a settled receipt is self-consistent but not necessarily correct, and because GoldenFloat ops are deterministic and bit-exact any challenger can recompute a single op and settle the dispute by equality — no bisection needed.

Outcome codes: HONEST 0, SLASH 1, MALFORMED 2, STALE 3, FAMILY_MISMATCH 4, INDETERMINATE 5, RUNG_MISMATCH 6. Format families FMT_GF_BINARY 0 and FMT_GFT 1, matching tri_compute_receipt.

Build the resolver in layers, each with a comment naming the hole it closes:
- Bare honesty: `is_honest`, `resolve`, and the bond arithmetic — the executor's bond is forfeited on SLASH, the challenger wins it on SLASH and has its own stake burned on a frivolous challenge.
- Leaf anchoring: `challenge_binds` and `resolve_bound`, rejecting as MALFORMED any dispute whose recomputed receipt leaf differs from the leaf settlement paid on.
- Anti-replay: `dispute_is_fresh` requiring a strictly greater epoch, and `resolver_epoch_after` advancing the watermark only on a terminal HONEST or SLASH, so a griefer cannot jump it with a MALFORMED dispute at a high epoch.
- Family and rung guards: `family_matches`, `rung_matches`, and `resolve_full` / `resolve_full_rung` chaining freshness, then family, then rung, then the leaf-anchored recompute; plus 256-bit-anchored variants taking a precomputed leaf_match flag.
- BitNet disputes verifying both the ternary part and the GF value, in bare, full, d256 and quorum forms.
- Quorum: `quorum_threshold(n)` = floor(n/2)+1, `has_quorum_k`, three-node helpers, and a five-node generalisation counting agreement per vote and taking the maximum.
- Verifier accountability: dissent from a formed quorum burns that verifier's stake (no quorum, no penalty), and agreeing verifiers are paid a floor-division share of the burned total, so verification is self-funding and never over-issues.

Close with brace-form tests for fraud being slashed, fabricated operands rejected, replay as a no-op, watermark advancement only on resolution, family and rung confusion, the d256 anchors, a dishonest minority outvoted, indeterminate outcomes, dissenting-verifier slashing, the five-node economics, and BitNet needing both parts.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module TriComputeReceipt { ... }`) defining the TRI-NET compute-attesting receipt: the committed content and verification logic for sealing WORK, not just relayed bytes. State in the header that the Ed25519 signature itself stays a Rust crate primitive and that this spec is the single source of truth for what gets signed.

Constants: RECEIPT_GENESIS "TRCR", the golden-ratio mixing constant R_C and a decorrelating second-lane seed R_C2; the SHA-256 preimage constants TAG_RECEIPT, SHA_PAD and DIGEST_MSG_BITS 288; the ledger constants TAG_LEDGER, LEDGER_GENESIS, LEDGER_MSG_BITS 608, MERKLE_MSG_BITS 512 and TAG_INPUT; the GF selectors GF_ADD 0x10, GF_MUL 0x11 and GF16; the families FMT_GF_BINARY and FMT_GFT; and the ratified GF-T ladder rungs Et = 4, 6, 9, 14.

Primitives `rotl` and `mix32`. Then:
- `receipt_leaf(executor, task, in_hash, out, epoch)` folding every field so changing any one changes the leaf; `receipt_step` chaining append-only; `verify_leaf` and `verify_chain3` recomputing from genesis.
- A second lane `receipt_leaf_hi` with different rotations and seed, and `verify_leaf64` requiring both lanes to match.
- `receipt_leaf_bound` folding in an unspoofable per-chip device_id, noting that 0 is the not-silicon-attested sentinel on the current openXC7 flow.
- `sign_digest` binding device, both lanes and the prior chain head, and `sign_digest_req` also binding the A2A request id so a signed receipt cannot be reattached to another task assignment.
- `digest_pre(idx, ...)` laying out the canonical single-block SHA-256 preimage: domain tag, the eight request-bound fields, then padding and length.
- GF attestation: `receipt_leaf_gf` folding width, op selector and operands; `receipt_leaf_gf_fmt` adding the family; `receipt_leaf_gf_rung` adding Et so a GF-T64 compute cannot be replayed as a cheaper GF-T16 one.
- `chain_step_full`, plus `ledger_entry_pre`, `merkle_pair_pre`, `input_digest_pre` and `verify_chain3_full`.

Finish with brace-form tests covering leaf verification, tamper evidence, chain determinism and order sensitivity, independent 64-bit lanes, device and request binding, GF op and family binding, distinct rung attestations, wrong-rung geometry being caught, and the layout and domain separation of every SHA-256 preimage.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect using the hyphenated semicolon module form (`module sacred-drowsy_ret;`) for sacred opcode 0xEC, DROWSY_RET — the power-state return instruction.

Constants: OP_DROWSY_RET 0xEC; three-bit state and reason fields; the states ACTIVE 0, LIGHT 1, DEEP 2, OFF 3, HIBERNATE 4, CRITICAL 5 with DROWSY_MAX 6; the return reasons WAKE 0, TIMER 1, INTERRUPT 2, ERROR 3, POWER 4, MANUAL 5 with RET_MAX 6; and WAKE_CYCLES 100 and DEEP_WAKE_CYCLES 1000.

Types: `DrowsyState` and `RetReason` as `enum(u8)` over those constants; `DrowsyConfig` (enable_light, enable_deep, the two thresholds in ms, wake_irq_enable); `DrowsyStatus` (state, last_wake_cycle, drowsy_duration, wake_count, last_ret_reason); `WakeCondition` (irq_pending, timer_expired, power_good, manual_wake).

State predicates: is_active, is_drowsy (light or deep), is_off (off or hibernate), is_critical, can_enter_light (only from active), can_enter_deep (only from light), and `drowsy_wake_cycles` returning the light or deep cost and zero otherwise.

Config builders: `drowsy_config_init` (both levels on, 100 ms and 1000 ms thresholds, IRQ wake on), `drowsy_config_disable`, `drowsy_config_light_only(threshold_ms)`.

Status transitions all return a new DrowsyStatus: `enter_light` and `enter_deep` are no-ops unless the guard permits the transition; `wake` goes active, stamps the cycle, increments wake_count and records the reason; `enter_critical` records RetReason.error; `enter_off` clears the wake cycle and records RetReason.power. `drowsy_should_wake` fires on IRQ, timer or manual; `drowsy_can_wake_critical` needs good power plus a manual wake; `drowsy_wake_from_condition` prioritises interrupt, then timer, then manual, then a power fault. `drowsy_update_duration` zeroes the duration outside a drowsy state and otherwise increments it; `drowsy_check_threshold` decides whether a light state should deepen.

Encode the instruction as [OP:8][REASON:3][STATE:3][DURATION:16][PAD:2] with matching encode and decode functions.

Cover every constant, predicate, builder, transition, wake decision, duration update, threshold check and the encode/decode roundtrip with named `test "..."` blocks; add invariants for the state and reason ranges, positive wake cycles, deep costing more than light, the mutual exclusivity of the predicates, the config defaults, wake incrementing the count and setting active, and zero duration outside drowsy; then latency benches for each function.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect using the hyphenated semicolon module form (`module triformat-nf4;`) specifying NormalFloat4, a 4-bit quantisation format based on a normalised distribution.

Constants: BITS 4, LEVELS 8 non-zero levels, TOTAL_LEVELS 16, and three negative and three positive magnitude levels. Type alias `NF4 = u8`, holding the 4-bit code in the low bits: one sign bit at position 2 and a two-bit magnitude index, with index 0 reserved for zero.

Declare two eight-entry f32 level tables — a plain one at 0, 1/3, 2/3, 1 mirrored negative, and a phi-optimised one at 0, 0.4167, 0.75, 1.0 mirrored negative, both with a duplicate zero in the last slot for rounding tie-breaks — and export the phi-optimised table as QUANTIZATION_LEVELS.

Conversions: `nf4_from_f32` returns zero for NaN and infinity, saturates outside [-1, 1], treats magnitudes below 0.2 as zero, and otherwise buckets at 0.58 and 0.87 before applying the sign bit; plus `nf4_from_f64`, `nf4_from_i8` (normalising by 127), `nf4_to_f32` (table lookup on the low three bits), `nf4_to_f64` and `nf4_to_i8`.

Arithmetic — add, sub, mul, div — dequantises to f32, operates and requantises; div returns zero for a near-zero divisor. Utilities: is_zero, is_negative, is_positive, abs (magnitude bits only), neg (zero stays zero), is_equal, is_greater, is_less, max, min, clamp, lerp, magnitude, l1_distance, l2_distance and scale.

Cover the surface with named `test "..."` blocks: quantisation at every magnitude band and both signs, saturation past the extremes, NaN and both infinities, dequantisation and roundtrips, the i8 conversions, each arithmetic operator including the divide-by-zero guard, every predicate, abs and neg, the comparisons, max/min/clamp/lerp, magnitude, both distances and scaling. Add invariants for the constants and table length, zero's classification, the sign symmetry of abs and neg, non-negative and symmetric distances, and the ordering bounds of max and min; finish with latency benches for the two hot conversions.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect using the hyphenated semicolon module form (`module gf16-to-posit16;`) specifying a GoldenFloat16 to Posit16 (unum 1.0) converter.

Constants: the GF16 layout — 16 bits, sign at bit 15, 6 exponent bits, 9 mantissa bits, bias 31 — and the Posit16 layout — 16 bits, ES 1, a maximum useed exponent of 7, 2 regime bits and 12 mantissa bits; plus MAX_EXP_DIFF 5.

Types: `Gf16` as a packed struct of u1 sign, u6 exp and u9 mant; `Posit16` wrapping a u16; `PositComponents` (sign, regime, exponent, mantissa); `ConversionResult` (bits, overflow, underflow, inexact); and `ConversionConfig` (round_mode, clamp_overflow).

GF16 side: `gf16_from_bits` / `gf16_to_bits`, the classifiers is_zero, is_subnormal, is_normal, is_infinity and is_nan, and `gf16_get_exp_biased` returning the unbiased exponent as i8.

Posit side: `posit16_from_bits` / `posit16_to_bits`, the recognisers is_zero, is_one, is_neg_one and is_naR, `posit16_get_sign`, and `posit16_decode`, which two's-complements a negative posit, counts the bounded regime run in either direction, skips the terminating bit, then extracts the ES exponent bits and the mantissa.

Conversion: `conversion_config_init` (round-to-nearest, clamping on). `gf16_to_posit16_raw` maps zero, infinity and NaN to their posit encodings first, then maps the GF16 exponent onto a regime and exponent, clamps the regime to [-14, 14], and assembles sign, regime run, ES bits and the mantissa shifted from 9 to 12 bits. `gf16_to_posit16_with_result` returns those bits with overflow and underflow flags derived from the exponent range plus an inexact flag, clamping to the signed maximum when overflow and clamp_overflow coincide. Add the wrappers `gf16_to_posit16`, `gf16_bits_to_posit16_bits` and its with-result form.

Cover it with named `test "..."` blocks over the constants, both bit roundtrips, every classifier and recogniser, the config defaults, conversion of zero, infinity, NaN and sign preservation, the bit-level wrappers, and the with-result flags for clamped and unclamped overflow. Add invariants for the field-width sums, both roundtrips, the special posit encodings and the special-value mappings; finish with latency benches for every entry point.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module ast { ... }`) defining the abstract syntax tree for TRI-27 assembly, shared by the lexer, parser and backends.

Declare `TokenType` as an `enum(u8)` with explicit numbering: punctuation and operators from 0, the use / const / data / code keywords and data directives, the TDD-inside-spec section keywords (test, invariant, bench, verify, expected, setup, rationale, measure, target), literals and identifiers from 40, the opcode tokens from 60 through 92, and the high-level spec keywords (spec, rule, given, when, then, assert, and, expect) from 93.

Declare `NodeType` covering the program structure, constants, instructions and every TDD node. `ASTNode` carries node_type, line, column and source_file, and every node embeds it. `Program` is the root: an optional spec declaration, constants, data and code sections, the optional test / invariant / bench sections, and the export and import lists. Add ConstDef, DataSection, DataDecl, CodeSection (instructions plus a label-to-index map), Instruction, a ten-value `Opcode` enum from MOV to HALT, Operand with an OperandType tag, and the four operand payload structs — registers 0-25 general with 26 as zero, immediates, label references and base-plus-offset memory.

Model the TDD nodes too: TestCase, InvariantDecl, BenchDecl (optional target plus a units field), and the high-level SpecDecl with its TestBlock, given/when/then/and clauses, AssertStmt, RuleDecl and ExpectClause.

Finally define TypeInfo, Symbol, a scoped `SymbolTable` whose lookup falls back to the parent, a `CompilerContext` carrying the root, symbol table, errors, warnings and the current `CompilationPhase`, the error and warning records, and the context helpers for adding and counting errors and warnings and exporting symbols.

Close with tests pinning the numeric value of specific enum members and the symbol table's empty and one-entry states; invariants on the enum sizes, the ordering of the compilation phases, location info on every node and the parent fallback in lookup; and benches for node creation and symbol lookup.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect using the hyphenated semicolon module form (`module sacred-lane_precheck;`) for sacred opcode 0xDF, the LUT lookup precheck: it validates lane readiness, checks LUT access permission and prepares the address before the lookup issues.

Constants: OP_LUT_LOOKUP 0xDF, LANE_COUNT 8, LUT_DEPTH 256, LUT_ADDR_BITS 8, LANE_ID_BITS 3, the lane states IDLE 0, READY 1, BUSY 2, ERROR 3, and CHECK_PASS 1 / CHECK_FAIL 0.

Types: `LaneStatus` as an `enum(u8)` over the four states; `PrecheckFlags` as a `packed struct(u8)` of lut_enabled, lane_valid, address_valid, permission_ok and four reserved bits; `PrecheckResult` (lane_id, status, flags, lut_address, error_code); and `LaneConfig` (enabled, lut_base, lut_mask, priority).

Status helpers: lane_is_valid (id below LANE_COUNT) plus is_ready, is_busy, is_error and is_idle.

`precheck_lane(lane_id, lut_addr, config)` computes all four flags, then assigns the first failing condition an error code in a fixed priority order — invalid lane 1, invalid address 2, permission denied 3, LUT disabled 4 — and zeroes the returned address unless the lane came out ready. `precheck_all_lanes` prechecks each selected lane and leaves the unselected ones idle with cleared flags. Add `precheck_pass`, `precheck_fail`, `precheck_any_pass`, `precheck_all_pass`, `precheck_count_passed` and `precheck_get_ready_lanes` returning a bitmask.

Address helpers: `lut_address_valid` (in range, LUT enabled, masked address below the mask), `lut_address_masked` and `lut_address_offset` saturating at zero below the base. Encode the instruction as [OP:8][LANE:3][ADDR:5] with matching encode and decode functions, the decoder returning an anonymous struct.

Cover the surface with named `test "..."` blocks — the predicates, a passing precheck and each of the four failure paths, any/all/count/ready-mask over an eight-lane result set, the address helpers and the encode/decode roundtrip — plus invariants on the constants, the lane id range, pass and fail being opposites, ready excluding busy, error excluding ready, and the bounds on the pass count and ready mask; finish with latency benches for the precheck entry points and the encode/decode pair.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module BandwidthAllocator { ... }`) for fair bandwidth distribution and QoS across network flows. This module has no structs: every record is packed into a u32 with explicit shifts and masks, and each packed field gets a matching accessor.

Constants: MAX_FLOWS 8, TOTAL_BANDWIDTH 1000 units per tick, MIN_BANDWIDTH 10, MAX_BANDWIDTH 500, and the priority levels PRIORITY_LOW 1, PRIORITY_MEDIUM 2, PRIORITY_HIGH 3 — declare them explicitly, and note in a comment that the requirement tests referenced them while they were undeclared, which made the generated code uncompilable in every backend.

`create_flow_requirement` packs [id:8][priority:2][min_bw:10][current_bw:12]; `create_allocation_state` packs [allocated:11][pending:8][fair_share:9][last_update:4]. Both get a full set of getters.

Store the eight flows in a real `[u32; 8]` array via `create_flow_array` and a bounds-checked `get_flow_req`, and note why: the previous u64 container packed 32-bit requirements at 8-bit strides, so every read overlapped its neighbours.

`calculate_fair_share` divides total bandwidth by the flow count, guarding zero. `allocate_bandwidth` branches on the declared priority constants — high gets its minimum plus 70% of what is available, medium a two-way fair share, low only its minimum — then clamps to the available bandwidth, to MAX_BANDWIDTH and up to the minimum before folding the result into a new allocation state; comment that the old branches keyed on 0 and 1, values no constant produces, so every high-priority caller fell into the low-priority arm. Add `needs_more_bandwidth`, `update_flow_bandwidth` clamping between the flow minimum and MAX_BANDWIDTH, `count_active_flows`, `find_reclaimable_bandwidth` (allocated minus the sum in use, floored at zero) and `prioritize_bandwidth` redistributing an equal share across all eight slots.

Write brace-form tests with message-carrying asserts for both packing roundtrips, fair share in the normal and zero-flow cases, allocation at each priority, both branches of needs_more_bandwidth, bandwidth updates against the minimum and maximum, active-flow counting on a full and a partial array, reclaimable bandwidth, and the even distribution from prioritize_bandwidth.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module anomaly_detector { ... }`) for behavioural anomaly detection over network metrics. The module uses no structs: records are packed into u32 with explicit shifts and masks, each with matching accessors.

Constants: MAX_METRICS 16, BASELINE_WINDOW 8, ANOMALY_THRESHOLD 30, SEVERITY_HIGH 80, SEVERITY_MEDIUM 50, and the anomaly types SPIKE 0, DROP 1, PATTERN 2, TREND 3.

`create_metric_reading(metric_id, value, timestamp, confidence)` packs four bytes with getters for each. `create_anomaly_report` packs [id:8][severity:8][type:2][confidence:14] with its own getters.

Statistics: `calculate_baseline` averages the metric values over the first `count` readings; `calculate_variance` returns the mean absolute deviation from that baseline. Both guard a zero count.

Detectors: `detect_spike` and `detect_drop` fire when the deviation from baseline exceeds three times the variance, falling back to ANOMALY_THRESHOLD when the variance is zero. `detect_pattern` needs at least four samples and fires when two or more consecutive triples alternate direction. `detect_trend` needs four samples and fires when more than 80% of the step-to-step moves go one way. `calculate_severity` bands the absolute deviation into 90, 60 or 30.

`detect_anomaly` returns 0 below BASELINE_WINDOW samples, otherwise computes baseline and variance and tries spike, drop, pattern and trend in that order, building a report with the matching severity and returning 0 when nothing fires. Add `is_critical_anomaly`, `get_anomaly_description` mapping the type to a code, `correlate_metrics` returning the percentage of steps where two histories moved the same non-zero direction, `detect_coordinated_attack` firing on two or more critical anomalies, and `calculate_anomaly_confidence` weighting severity 30%, base 50% and historical 20%, capped at 100.

Write brace-form tests with message-carrying asserts for both packing roundtrips; a baseline-and-variance case over eight readings alternating 100 and 120 that must give a baseline of 110 and a deviation of 10; spike and drop detection at that variance, each with a firing and a non-firing case; and the three severity bands.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect (`module docs_generator { ... }`) for multi-format documentation output generation. The module uses no structs: every record is packed into a u32 with explicit shifts and masks, and each packed field gets its own accessor.

Constants: MAX_SECTIONS 16, MAX_TABLES 8, MAX_REFERENCES 32, OUTPUT_BUFFER_SIZE 4096; the output formats MARKDOWN 0, HTML 1, PDF 2, TEXT 3, JSON 4; the HTML tag types H1, H2, H3, P, TABLE, DIV numbered 1 to 6; and the link types INTERNAL, EXTERNAL, API, EXAMPLE.

Packed records, each with a constructor and getters: an output format of [format_id:4][version:8][compression:4][encoding:16]; a document section of [section_id:8][level:4][content_length:8][subsection_count:12]; a TOC entry of [section_id:8][level:4][page_number:8][title_id:12]; an HTML tag of [tag_type:8][content_id:8][attributes:16]; a reference link of [source:8][target:8][type:4][anchor:12]; a code block of [language:8][code_id:8][line_count:16]; a data table of four bytes plus a row generator; an index entry of [term_id:8][location:8][frequency:8][importance:8]; a page layout of the four margins as bytes; and metadata of [title_id:8][author_id:8][date:8][version:8].

`generate_markdown_header(level, title_id)` selects the byte pattern 0x23, 0x2323 or 0x232323 for heading levels 1 to 3 and packs it above the title id.

`calculate_document_stats` walks the sections estimating words at five characters each and pages at three hundred words, counts a table for any section with subsections, and packs the four totals. `format_document` sums the section content lengths, adds the margin overhead, and adds a per-section allowance depending on whether the format is HTML or Markdown. `generate_complete_document` builds metadata and a default layout, sizes the TOC, body and index, and packs the total with the section and function counts. `validate_documentation` compares actual against expected counts and packs the match flags with a quality score and a completeness figure.

Finish with two brace-form tests using message-carrying asserts: a roundtrip through the output-format packing on all four fields, and the Markdown header prefixes and title id at levels 1 and 3.
